Experimental HEVC mode. Requires a compatible hardware encoder on this phone and H.265 support in the receiver. Uses the same /webrtc and /whep addresses with optional Opus audio. If playback fails, select H.264 + WebRTC. There is no automatic codec fallback; lower bandwidth or latency is not guaranteed.

JPEG enables the JPEG Browser and MJPEG addresses with identical image bytes. WebRTC enables /webrtc and /whep using the selected H.264 or experimental H.265 codec. H.265 needs a compatible receiver.
WebRTC · go2rtc source · tap to copy

For go2rtc, copy the go2rtc source address from the main screen into your stream configuration. Keep the webrtc: prefix and /whep path. /webrtc is an HTML player, not a direct media source. Video uses the selected H.264 or experimental H.265 codec; optional microphone audio uses Opus. The relay and final player must support that codec. Reconnect the source after changing codec or enabling/disabling audio.

Use a trusted local network. JPEG and signaling use unencrypted HTTP; WebRTC media uses DTLS-SRTP.
Focus and zoom on a tripod

Automatic keeps focusing as the scene changes. Focus & lock focuses once and holds until you tap Refocus or reopen the camera. Manual starts at the measured lens position and lets you adjust from far to near; it remembers that position for this camera. Distance labels are approximate and appear only when the camera reports calibrated units. Zoom and focus affect preview and all stream formats. Digital zoom cannot recover missing detail, and objects closer than the lens can focus must be moved farther away.
This camera has a fixed-focus lens.
Far ← → Near. Manual holds the lens position and is saved for this camera. Move the phone farther away if the object is too close to focus.
Locked, but focus was not found. Move farther away or tap Refocus.
Focus locked. Refocus finds a new distance; reopening the camera focuses again.
Autofocus follows the scene. Choose Manual to hold the current lens position, or Focus & lock to focus once.
Zoom affects preview and every stream. Hardware determines the range; digital zoom magnifies pixels and can reduce detail.

This edition updates the original app with modern Android SDKs, saved settings, JPEG streaming and H.264 + WebRTC, plus experimental H.265. Built for Android 17 / API 37.
Rate above: JPEG data produced by the camera.
Choose a format. Keep the picture flowing.
Both addresses carry the exact same JPEG image bytes, resolution and quality. The difference is how the receiver handles them.
For OBS Browser Source. The receiver confirms each decoded frame. One frame travels while only the newest frame waits. Slow reception skips old frames instead of growing the queue.
For OBS Media Source, VLC and compatible tools. This standard stream remains available in JPEG mode. The player controls its own buffer; the phone cannot confirm when it displays a frame.

Recommended WebRTC format for browser and OBS compatibility at /webrtc. The camera feeds a hardware H.264 encoder directly, with no JPEG intermediate. WebRTC adapts bitrate and may reduce FPS to maintain resolution. Optional phone microphone audio uses Opus.

Choose one active format on the main screen. JPEG retains its quality control and camera sizes. Each WebRTC codec shows sizes supported by the camera and its compatible hardware encoder, with a separate bitrate control. H.265 is an additional test mode; H.264 remains the recommended WebRTC option.

The limit is a ceiling, not a promise of constant quality or bandwidth use. Allow roughly twice that rate per receiver as practical headroom. Actual use adapts to the scene and connection. This is not a speed test.
JPEG: receiver cycle ≤80% of a frame interval and fewer than 2% skipped frames. WebRTC: connected, encoding at least 80% of captured FPS, with no reported encoder limitation.
JPEG: a longer cycle or 2–20% skipped frames. WebRTC: the encoder reports a bandwidth/CPU limit, or encoded FPS is lower than captured FPS.
JPEG: cycle exceeds two frame intervals, at least 20% of frames are skipped, or transfer stalls. For WebRTC, check connection state and the receiver if video stops.
No receiver, connection in progress, missing samples, or MJPEG without playback feedback. Color is a diagnostic hint, not a measurement of end-to-end delay.

JPEG receiver cycle includes transfer, decode, canvas draw and reply. WebRTC RTT measures the network round trip. Neither includes the complete camera-to-OBS/display/audio path. JPEG statistics use a recent two-second window; WebRTC uses its native sender reports.

Use Browser Source for /view (JPEG) or /webrtc (H.264; experimental H.265 requires a compatible receiver), with custom FPS set to 30. Stream rotation on the phone applies to all three addresses. Match the source to the rotated picture: for portrait Full HD use width 1080 and height 1920; for landscape use 1920×1080. A landscape source keeps the full portrait picture with side bars. Fit the source proportionally; do not stretch it or apply the same rotation again in OBS.

Close unused viewers and the previous camera source. For Browser Source, enable “Shutdown source when not visible” if hidden sources should disconnect. Multiple receivers each need bandwidth and WebRTC encoding resources.

For MJPEG in Media Source, start with Network Buffering = 0 MB. Raise it only if necessary for stability. WebRTC manages its jitter buffer automatically. More buffering adds delay and cannot repair a sustained bandwidth shortage.

Prefer Ethernet for the PC and strong 5/6 GHz Wi-Fi or a wired connection for the phone. Internet upload speed is not LAN capacity. WebRTC connects directly on the LAN without a public STUN/TURN server; network isolation can prevent connection.

WebRTC can send the phone microphone with video. Enable Microphone audio, grant permission, and enable Control audio via OBS in the Browser Source. A browser may require clicking Enable sound. Mute sends silence without restarting video; disabling audio releases capture and reconnects receivers. For a separate PC microphone, record a clap test in OBS. If audio is 150 ms early, apply +150 ms in Advanced Audio Properties → Sync Offset. Fix changing video delay before choosing an offset.

Estimates for one receiver, using the current scene and average JPEG size. The last column uses 2× headroom as a planning guideline, not a guarantee or a measured network speed. More detail or motion can increase JPEG sizes. Two receivers need roughly twice the total bandwidth. These FPS rows are calculations, not camera mode choices.
RemoteCam needs the camera and, on Android 17, local network access. If permission was permanently denied, enable it in system app settings.
Open controls or stop the camera
WebRTC rotation: manual angles start from upright portrait and stay fixed when you turn the phone. Applies immediately to receivers; the local camera preview is unchanged.

Rotation applies to both JPEG Browser and MJPEG. Manual angles start from upright portrait. The camera rotates the JPEG; if it only writes EXIF, the app rotates and re-encodes at quality 100 for compatible playback. That fallback can increase CPU use and bandwidth. Local preview is unchanged.
